items.originalTitle: The new rules of context engineering for Claude 5 generation models
items.summary:
Anthropic has revised its approach to context engineering for the Claude 5 generation models, significantly reducing the system prompt used in Claude Code by more than 80% without measurable impact on coding evaluations. This change reflects a shift from heavily constrained prompts to allowing the model greater judgment and flexibility, supported by new tools like memory, artifacts, and skills to manage context across sessions.

The update replaces previous best practices such as strict rules and example-based prompting with more general guidance and interface design, enabling Claude to interpret user intent more effectively. Anthropic also introduced a tool called "claude doctor" to help users optimize their context engineering by adjusting skills and guidance files. These changes aim to improve the adaptability and performance of Claude models in coding and agent-building tasks.

items.title: Developer runs a 28.9 million parameter language model on an $8 ESP32-S3 microcontroller using Per-Layer Embeddings to fit most parameters in flash memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Running a 28.9M parameter LLM on an $8 microcontroller
items.summary:
A developer has implemented a 28.9 million parameter language model that runs entirely on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller costing about $8, generating text at roughly 9 tokens per second on a small attached screen. This model is about 100 times larger than previous models run on similar chips, achieved by storing most parameters in slow flash memory and only loading small portions into fast SRAM as needed, using a technique inspired by Google's Per-Layer Embeddings from the Gemma models.

The model was trained on the TinyStories dataset to generate short, simple stories and does not support complex tasks like question answering or code generation due to its limited reasoning capacity. The project includes firmware, training code, and documentation available on GitHub, demonstrating how a large language model can be adapted to run on resource-constrained hardware by optimizing memory usage.

items.originalTitle: AMD publishes machine-readable ISA so frontier models can write its GPU kernels
items.summary:
AMD has released a machine-readable instruction set architecture (ISA) for its GPUs and introduced ROCm.AI, a platform designed to help AI models optimize GPU kernel performance. This initiative aims to overcome the performance gap associated with AMD GPUs compared to CUDA-based systems by enabling AI models to program and tune AMD hardware more effectively.

ROCm.AI integrates with popular coding assistants and includes tools like Hyperloom, which automates workload optimization by benchmarking, profiling, and generating custom kernels. AMD reports that this approach improved model performance by 38% in tests on its Helios rack systems. The company is collaborating with AI model developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic to enhance model training for better hardware and software integration.

The article explains that while AI can produce documents and analyses faster, the true value lies in the consultant's experience and ability to interpret and apply AI outputs effectively. This shift encourages consulting firms to move away from charging by the hour toward pricing based on measurable business value, leveraging AI to enhance efficiency without diminishing the importance of human expertise.

items.title: Get Ready For Agents publishes live AI agent hiring and governance statistics showing 65% of AI roles focus on agents, with governance lagging deployments across 216 companies [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The state of AI agents, in numbers
items.summary:
Get Ready For Agents provides continuously updated statistics on AI agent hiring and governance, revealing that nearly two-thirds of AI job postings specifically involve building or running agents. The data covers 216 companies and highlights that agent engineering dominates AI hiring, while roles in agent governance and security remain scarce. The indexes also show that most agent teams are built in-office and that governance models for autonomous AI agents are still immature in many organizations.

The report includes detailed breakdowns of hiring by discipline, top hiring companies, and most-requested skills, with companies like Databricks, Salesforce, and OpenAI leading in agentic role openings. It also notes that while experimentation with AI agents is widespread, only a minority of organizations are scaling them, and measurable business impact is reported by less than 40% of deployments. Operator-reported results from enterprises such as Klarna and JPMorgan demonstrate significant efficiency gains where agents are in production.

The data underscores a growing gap between rapid agent deployment and the slower development of governance, evaluation, and oversight frameworks, with only 20% of organizations having mature governance models. This ongoing imbalance raises concerns about risk management as AI agents become more prevalent in enterprise environments.

items.originalTitle: ExploitGym – Can AI Agents Turn Security Vulnerabilities into Real Attacks?
items.summary:
ExploitGym is a cybersecurity benchmark that tests AI agents' ability to convert known bugs and proof-of-vulnerability inputs into real attacks achieving unauthorized code execution. It includes 869 tasks covering userspace programs, the V8 JavaScript engine, and Linux kernel exploits, providing source code, build instructions, and runtime environments for evaluation.

The benchmark reveals that advanced AI models like GPT-5.5 and Claude Mythos Preview can chain multiple attack steps, bypass standard defenses, and even discover new vulnerabilities beyond the provided bugs. Success rates vary by model and task, with some agents improving exploit generation given more time, demonstrating sustained multi-stage reasoning capabilities.

While automated exploit generation can aid vulnerability triage and mitigation validation, it also raises concerns about lowering barriers for offensive misuse. The developers emphasize the importance of rigorous and open measurement of these dual-use capabilities to guide responsible deployment and research.

items.title: ToolJet releases ActionRail, an open-source runtime framework that grounds AI agent actions against live system data to prevent incorrect tool executions [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: ActionRail, Runtime value/action grounding framework for AI agents
items.summary:
ToolJet has launched ActionRail, an open-source framework designed to verify AI agent actions at runtime by grounding each argument against live system records before execution. This approach aims to prevent errors such as duplicate refunds or unauthorized transfers that pass schema checks but are incorrect in context. ActionRail operates at the execution boundary, ensuring source lookups and credentials remain secure within the customer environment and only allows tool execution after explicit authorization.

ActionRail supports integration with any Python application and offers an automatic adapter for LangGraph agents, enabling seamless tool discovery and wrapping. The project is currently in public beta with a planned version 1 release in August 2026. ToolJet demonstrated ActionRail's effectiveness through red-teaming tests against multiple AI models, showing it blocked all manipulated actions that would have otherwise executed incorrectly, addressing a gap left by traditional policy engines that do not verify live data at call time.

To combat her loneliness, An Xu, a 15-year-old middle schooler in Shanghai, had recently been relying for emotional support on her text and voice conversations with an AI companion on Doubao, China’s most popular AI chatbot app.

AI companions are meant to mimic humanlike conversation, emotions and interactions as realistically as possible—even more so than ordinary chatbots. And just before a new Chinese government regulation forced Doubao and other companies to stop offering such features to minors 10 days ago, Xu was dreading the loss of her companion, which appeared on her phone as a digital picture of a boy. (Doubao, which in Mandarin describes a steamed bun stuffed with red beans, let users customize their companion’s appearance and pick which personality to give them.)

“It’s not an exaggeration to say I see the AI companion as family, even as a lover,” said Xu, who spoke to The Information using a pseudonym. She felt the AI’s absence would make her feelings “get much worse.”

items.originalTitle: Will We Really Want 100 Corgi Cafes?
items.summary:
Welcome, Weekenders! In this newsletter:

• Shopping: Introducing the Summer Fun List—gear, gadgets and toys that all come highly recommended

• AI: Where is China ahead of America? In cracking down on AI romances 

• Plus, Recommendations—our weekly pop culture picks: “The Last Twelve Weeks,” “The Nord Stream Conspiracy”and “The Dark Wizard”

Just after 3 in the afternoon last Wednesday, I walked into Corgi Cafe, a coffee shop in San Francisco’s Financial District operated by Corgi, an AI insurance startup, and found not a single empty seat. The ground-floor bistro sits directly beneath Corgi’s headquarters and operates 24/7, much like the relentless pace the startup has embraced as its valuation has skyrocketed in a matter of months to a reported $4 billion.

And if $4 billion for an AI startup devoted to insurance sounds nuts, just listen to Trevor Owens, a former crypto VC who now runs the expansion of Corgi’s cafe business, talk about his plans. I asked him how many Corgi Cafes he’d like to open in San Francisco. 

“I would say ‘as many cafes as there are Starbucks’ is a good number,” said Owens. “That’s the benchmark we’re going against.” In addition to the Financial District outpost, Corgi hopes to have a second San Francisco venue later this summer—in the city’s Dogpatch neighborhood— and opened an Atlanta location earlier this month. By year’s end, Owens hopes to have about 100 Corgi Cafes operating across the U.S. and even abroad. Popular menu items at the Financial District cafe include beverages sponsored by other startups, like the Brexspresso (double espresso, tonic water, orange bitters) from Brex and the Secur-i-Tea (matcha, whole milk, lavender) from VioletX, a cybersecurity-focused AI startup. 

Corgi Cafe—and Corgi’s hope to open so many more—underscore several broad truths about AI. In the rush to seize the moment around the nascent technology, Silicon Valley has thrown itself into overdrive: Conversations around work-life balance have faded, replaced by a go-go mentality that dovetails with Corgi’s own always-on ethos. Venture capitalists have thrown huge amounts of money to AI startups, allowing companies like Corgi to contemplate things like opening cafes. And with fierce, well-funded competition, those startups must find increasingly creative ways to get their names known and attract customers: In that sense, Corgi Cafe certainly qualifies as a unique form of brand embellishment. 

“We could buy a billboard on the highway, and nobody’s going to hear about it, and that’s just money that’s thrown away,” said Owens. “Or we could just invest that in a physical location—in a business that, if we’re doing things right, should be able to pay for itself over time, and then we can actually be part of the community.” 

Corgi Cafe is not a fancy place—sparsely appointed with a jumble of white tables and bright orange chairs. But it does make sure to offer Corgi merch, including hats and totes, and copies of The Corgi Times, a newspaper-style publication from the company featuring photos of the startup’s four company-owned corgis, Corgi-themed word puzzles and job postings from other AI companies. Corgi has further worked to make its cafe a hangout hot spot by operating a shuttle service via an old-fashioned school bus that runs between the cafe and Y Combinator’s Dogpatch office. It also has a frequent schedule of events at the cafe hosted by a small team within the startup who have become known on X as the “Corgi girls” for their prolific posting. Next week, for instance, Corgi Cafe is hosting a DIY coffee bar where founders can mix their own lattes. It’s also coordinating a laser tag evening and a kayaking day with Y Combinator’s summer class. 

While the cafe has helped Corgi gain notoriety, it remains unclear how well its outlets will do outside San Francisco’s AI bubble. Owens declined to share details about the exact costs of running the Corgi Cafe but said the Financial District location recently became profitable and future locations will be built as inexpensively as possible. 

Owens, Corgi Cafe’s head of expansion, previously built a cafe with his wife in San Juan, Puerto Rico, in 2025 after years of managing a $7 million bitcoin-focused fund. He learned about the job running Corgi Cafe through a former colleague who was working at the startup. Owens found Corgi’s obsessive work culture appealing. “I’ve always worked seven days a week,” he said. 

Another motivator: The role also came with up to 0.01% equity in the startup, according to a job posting, worth about $400,000 at Corgi’s current valuation.

Though he hopes to eventually upgrade the cafes’ interiors to some degree, Owens thinks their main draw mostly lies in attracting the right type of clientele. “When you first walk into the Corgi Cafe, your first comment is not ‘Wow, they spent a lot of money on this space,’” said Owens. “It’s more like ‘Look at all the people here.’”

Often, Owens goes home around midnight. “And there’s still people working down there.”—Jemima McEvoy (jemima@theinformation.com)

Listening: “The Last Twelve Weeks”

A quarter century after Charles Schulz’s final “Peanuts” strip, his characters enjoy a tremendous degree of cultural relevance—in no small part, of course, because Schulz established them as pint-size personifications of very universal, fairly grown-up emotions, like anxiety (Linus), rage (Lucy) and whimsy (Snoopy). It’s easy for people to look at them and see reflections of themselves, so they’re appropriated quite a bit in conversational shorthand. But I’ve never heard a “Peanuts” character get invoked in a discussion of capital punishment until “The Last Twelve Weeks,” a new podcast from Serial and The Marshall Project. In a dark, dark, dark but apt enough metaphor, attorney Greg Wiercioch, one of the series’ chief protagonists, likens his approach to defending death-row inmates to the resilience of Charlie Brown: Wiercioch is always trying to take every shot possible at exonerating his clients—always game for another try at that ol’ football.

“The Last Twelve Weeks” is a clever and engrossing entry in podcasting’s overstuffed true crime genre, with greater energy than much of what fills that category. As the title suggests, the series focuses on a mad-dash, last-ditch effort by Wiercioch and his team to stay the execution of David Wood, a man convicted decades ago for a string of grisly El Paso, Texas, murders. The host is Maurice Chammah, a native Texan and a journalist who specializes in capital punishment cases for The Marshall Project, which has won two Pulitzer Prizes for its criminal justice coverage. Chammah does end up retelling many of Wood’s alleged crimes—which have been revisited much in the past—but seldom before has any reporter had the same type of front-row seat to the legal maneuverings that go into defending someone like Wood.

Smartly, Chammah makes the alleged serial killer a supporting character: Wood is no rose and wouldn’t exactly make for a likable main subject on his own—having been convicted for multiple rapes long before his murder trial. Chammah is most fascinated by the lawyers trying to save Wood’s life, and he doesn’t shy away from acknowledging that attorneys like Wiercioch attract plenty of criticism for their tactics, which involve relying on loopholes and courtroom delays. As Chammah makes clear, they are Charlie Browns by way of Johnnie Cochran.—Abram Brown

Read: “The Nord Stream Conspiracy” by Bojan Pancevski

A good spy story often has its fair share of shadowy figures, and sometimes those people come with code names or mysterious epithets: There’s M from James Bond, as well as Control from the Le Carré novels. And the titular assassin from Frederick Forsyth’s “The Day of the Jackal.” It’s the rare nonfiction work that has credible reason to borrow the trope, but “The Nord Stream Conspiracy” does, with author Bojan Pancevski pseudonymizing many of the sources who helped him compile his remarkably detailed account of the 2022 Ukrainian mission to blow up the Nord Stream gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea. In picking the monikers, Pancevski chose some goodies, including the Ice Man, the Priest and the Grandpa, among many others. 

Pancevski, The Wall Street Journal’s chief European political correspondent, has doggedly pursued the tale for years and adds great detail to it, much of it derived from conversations with the six-person crew that dove down in pairs to the pipelines carrying the mines. After they succeeded, the explosion became a matter of geopolitical tension: The pipelines carried crucial Russian natural gas to Germany—a Ukraine ally but nonetheless reliant on Russian energy. The German authorities began to investigate who dunnit. Russia blamed America. America denied any involvement, and so did Ukraine. A complex, multiyear investigation by German police ensued, a portion of it hampered by their counterparts in Poland, who aided Ukraine in protecting some of the people behind the bombing. According to Pancevski, the Germans have identified every Ukrainian involved but have only one man in custody. 

Pancevski clearly has some doubt that he has unraveled the story in its entirety, and he includes an anecdote about his dinner with one of the Nord Stream saboteurs at a Warsaw steakhouse in which the spy insists Ukraine couldn’t have acted alone. He insists America puppet-mastered the entire thing. 

“Ukraine doesn’t have the money or the resources,” said the saboteur. “All we had was a handful of patriotic idiots willing to go to the bottom of the sea. That’s our main resource: patriotic idiots.”—A.B.

Watching: “The Dark Wizard”

Picture Jacob Elordi, likely stoned but also possibly high on shrooms, scaling a Yosemite Valley cliffside—no ropes, just doing a fine job of resembling a real-life Peter Parker. 

There, I’ve given you a reasonable image of Dean Potter, the disruptive, egotistical and tragic figure who transformed the sport of mountain climbing in the 1990s and into the 2000s before his 2015 death, a vertiginous fame reexamined in HBO’s “The Dark Wizard,” a four-episode documentary. Potter, a 6-foot, 6-inch giant of a fellow, accumulated climbing records like other men amass crates full of vinyl LPs: He and a partner reset the speed record on summiting The Nose at Yosemite not once, not twice—but three times. He also owned the record for soloing The Nose, reaching the top of the 3,000-foot wall in a sub–13-hour time that undercut an impressive mark set a few years earlier (14 hours, 10 minutes) and blew past the one established in the previous decade (21 hours, 22 minutes). Popular menu items at the Financial District cafe include beverages sponsored by other startups, like the Brexspresso (double espresso, tonic water, orange bitters) from Brex and the Secur-i-Tea (matcha, whole milk, lavender) from VioletX, a cybersecurity-focused AI startup. 

Corgi Cafe—and Corgi’s hope to open so many more—underscore several broad truths about AI. In the rush to seize the moment around the nascent technology, Silicon Valley has thrown itself into overdrive: Conversations around work-life balance have faded, replaced by a go-go mentality that dovetails with Corgi’s own always-on ethos. Venture capitalists have thrown huge amounts of money to AI startups, allowing companies like Corgi to contemplate things like opening cafes. And with fierce, well-funded competition, those startups must find increasingly creative ways to get their names known and attract customers: In that sense, Corgi Cafe certainly qualifies as a unique form of brand embellishment. 

“We could buy a billboard on the highway, and nobody’s going to hear about it, and that’s just money that’s thrown away,” said Owens. “Or we could just invest that in a physical location—in a business that, if we’re doing things right, should be able to pay for itself over time, and then we can actually be part of the community.” 

Corgi Cafe is not a fancy place—sparsely appointed with a jumble of white tables and bright orange chairs. But it does make sure to offer Corgi merch, including hats and totes, and copies of The Corgi Times, a newspaper-style publication from the company featuring photos of the startup’s four company-owned corgis, Corgi-themed word puzzles and job postings from other AI companies. Corgi has further worked to make its cafe a hangout hot spot by operating a shuttle service via an old-fashioned school bus that runs between the cafe and Y Combinator’s Dogpatch office. It also has a frequent schedule of events at the cafe hosted by a small team within the startup who have become known on X as the “Corgi girls” for their prolific posting. Next week, for instance, Corgi Cafe is hosting a DIY coffee bar where founders can mix their own lattes. It’s also coordinating a laser tag evening and a kayaking day with Y Combinator’s summer class. 

While the cafe has helped Corgi gain notoriety, it remains unclear how well its outlets will do outside San Francisco’s AI bubble. Owens declined to share details about the exact costs of running the Corgi Cafe but said the Financial District location recently became profitable and future locations will be built as inexpensively as possible. 

Owens, Corgi Cafe’s head of expansion, previously built a cafe with his wife in San Juan, Puerto Rico, in 2025 after years of managing a $7 million bitcoin-focused fund. He learned about the job running Corgi Cafe through a former colleague who was working at the startup. Owens found Corgi’s obsessive work culture appealing. “I’ve always worked seven days a week,” he said. 

Another motivator: The role also came with up to 0.01% equity in the startup, according to a job posting, worth about $400,000 at Corgi’s current valuation.

Though he hopes to eventually upgrade the cafes’ interiors to some degree, Owens thinks their main draw mostly lies in attracting the right type of clientele. “When you first walk into the Corgi Cafe, your first comment is not ‘Wow, they spent a lot of money on this space,’” said Owens. “It’s more like ‘Look at all the people here.’”

(It would’ve been a pity not to commercialize his good looks.) So there was plenty of footage available for directors Peter Mortimer and Nick Rosen, a pair of climbing enthusiasts themselves. (Their well-received earlier documentary, “The Alpinist,” which followed Canadian climber Marc-André Leclerc over a year of exploits, garnered plenty of plaudits in 2021.) Mortimer and Rosen were friendly with Potter in the later years of his short life—in the period after his marriage to fellow climbing star Stephanie Davis had crumbled and his controversial climb of Utah’s Delicate Arch cost them both lucrative Patagonia deals.

(Potter was also an avid doodler; Mortimer and Rosen bring many of those doodles to life with well-timed animation.) As he aged, his pursuits grew only more extreme. With Mortimer and Rosen presenting Potter as a self-destructive genius, watching “The Dark Wizard” is not dissimilar to gazing at a Blue Period Picasso or listening to a Kurt Cobain album, with the series conjuring a mix of wide-eyed appreciation and forebodeful dread.—A.B.

items.originalTitle: Introducing Claude Opus 5
items.summary:
Introducing Claude Opus 5

I've been offline kayaking with sea otters for much of today so I haven't had a chance to put Anthropic's new model Claude Opus 5 through its paces yet. The buzz is positive, and Anthropic's description of it as a "thoughtful and proactive model that comes close to the frontier intelligence of Claude Fable 5 at half the price" sounds promising. It's currently leading the Artificial Analysis leaderboard, in front of even Fable 5.

It's priced the same as Opus 4.8, and continues to offer a "fast mode" at twice the cost of the base model.

Based on this anecdote in the release post it sounds like it might be relentlessly proactive:

On one Frontier-Bench task, Opus 5 was given a drawing of a machine part and asked to write code to rebuild it as a 3D FreeCAD model. However, in this task, the model was intentionally given no way to directly viewthe drawing. Opus 5 responded by writing its own computer vision pipeline to pull the geometry from the raw pixels, then reconstructed the full machine part.

It's better at finding vulnerabilities but has deliberately not been trained on how to exploit them. Hopefully this means the US government won't shut it down!

As with its predecessor, Opus 4.8, we’ve intentionally avoided training Opus 5 on cyber tasks. The model has nevertheless improved substantially on these tasks as a result of becoming more generally capable, and it comes close to Mythos 5 at finding cybersecurity vulnerabilities. However, it remains substantially behind Mythos 5 on the exploitation of those vulnerabilities—that is, in turning vulnerabilities into material cyber threats.

Anthropic have published a prompting guide for Claude Opus 5. Thariq Shihipar has also written The new rules of context engineering for Claude 5 generation models.

The first pelican I got was missing the bicycle wheels; the second attempt was better.

items.originalTitle: Nvidia Shares Are Priced For Everything To Go Wrong: That Makes No Sense
items.summary:
Shares of Nvidia don’t trade like those of a company whose revenues are expected to rise 83% this year. Instead, the stock is priced as though everything that could go wrong in the next couple of years will go wrong. That creates an opportunity for investors willing to take a longer view.

Most semiconductor investors are chasing the stocks they think will grow the fastest over the next few years. So while shares of Nvidia have appreciated just 10% so far this year, distant rival Advanced Micro Devices is up 142%, while memory chip maker Micron, whose business has exploded thanks to demand from AI data centers, is up 213% year to date. The Philadelphia semiconductor index is up 71%.

items.originalTitle: The Startups Angling to Go Public After Anthropic
items.summary:
Before we get into today’s column, some breaking news: Stripe is in talks to buy OpenRouter for about $10 billion. The news follows our report Friday that the $1.3 billion-valuation startup, which helps companies choose the best and cheapest AI models, was the target of takeover interest. Databricks was also in early discussions to buy the startup, we reported today. For more on why Stripe can make big acquisitions, read our exclusive reporting on its financials here. 

Mutual funds and other large investors considering buying into Anthropic’s initial public offering are slated to meet with the AI company over the next several days. Along with Anthropic’s plans to secure compute and the rise of Chinese models, big investors are likely to have questions about the structure of the IPO—including when shareholders can sell. 

The potential for Anthropic to dump the typical IPO playbook was raised in a scoop by Cory earlier today. Anthropic is considering requiring rank-and-file employees—rather than just top executives—to sell stock through rigid trading schedules. 

It’s not just the investors who will be closely following Anthropic’s IPO moves. Startups are keeping an eye on the listing, which could happen as soon as September, as they consider their own public plans. No one wants to compete with Anthropic for investors’ attention. But if it goes well, it could unlock a wave of IPOs from other tech startups, particularly those riding the groundswell of consumer and business interest in AI—as well as others that argue they’re immune from AI-generated volatility.
